issues.title: Spawn-per-connection is NOT built -- plan claims G1 is closeable in Phase 1 but forge.nova has zero spawn calls
issues.detail: The plan's entire concurrency claim ('10k concurrent connections, proven') rests on spawn-per-connection serving. But forge.nova (562 lines, HEAD 6835426) contains ZERO calls to spawn. The serve(), serve_arena(), serve_n_arena(), and serve_app() functions all call _handle_one/_handle_one_arena synchronously inside the accept loop. The comment at line 12 ('spawn per conn') is aspirational, not real. The arena model (_handle_one_arena) explicitly runs inside the accept loop, so arena_enter/arena_exit bracket a single synchronous request. Adding spawn INSIDE the arena path creates a correctness hazard: the arena is per-task (NovaTaskState), but the current code runs arena_enter on the ACCEPT task, not on a spawned child task. Converting to spawn-per-connection means the arena must be entered INSIDE the spawned task, which requires restructuring _handle_one_arena and re-proving the 'live_delta 16359 -> 0' result. This is not a '0 compiler changes' Tier-0 item -- it is a structural rearchitecture of the serve path that touches the arena/concurrency interaction, the most dangerous part of the system. If this stalls (arena corruption under concurrent spawned tasks), every Phase 1+ milestone is blocked.
issues.fix: Acknowledge spawn-per-connection as a Core prerequisite (not a 'pure NOVA Tier-0' change). Build and test it in isolation with arena + green scheduler interaction before any Forge Phase 1 work. Add it as Phase 0d with its own ASAN + green_scale gate.

issues.title: Phase 1 claims 'zero compiler changes' but 17 deliverables include at least 3 that need compiler work
issues.detail: Phase 1 item #7 (_coerce for bare-struct return) requires the return-site auto-JSON compiler hook. The plan acknowledges this in Phase 0's FORGE_DESIGN doc (section 4.3: 'this IS a compiler change') and in the FORGE_MASTER_PLAN module-1 description. But the execution plan's Phase 1 table says 'Core work: None beyond Phase 0 (all pure NOVA = Tier 0, no reconverge).' This is a contradiction. If the return-site hook is Phase 0, then Phase 0 is NOT 'NEARLY COMPLETE' -- it has an unbuilt compiler change that requires a Tier-3 gate (bootstrap reconverge). The plan also says Phase 0c (from_json typed-let) is 'DONE (forge_keystone_test proves it)' but the forge_keystone_test calls from_json with a known type at the let-site -- it does NOT test the handler-return-through-any path. These are different code paths. The plan conflates 'typed-let works' with 'handler return works,' and they are not the same thing.
issues.fix: Move the return-site auto-JSON hook explicitly into Phase 0 as a gated Tier-3 deliverable with its own reconverge. Do not start Phase 1 until the handler_return_json_test (which does not exist yet) passes. Rewrite Phase 1 to truly have zero compiler changes.

issues.title: Scope-exit RC has 1 FATAL + 6 HIGH adversary findings unresolved -- plan parallelizes it with Phase 3 as if it were bounded work
issues.detail: The plan says scope-exit RC '~4-5 iterations' and parallelizes it with Phase 3. But the SCOPE_EXIT_RC_DESIGN.md adversary review found 1 FATAL (double-free between S3 reassignment-drop and S4 scope-exit-drop) and 6 HIGH issues (leak in tight loops, per-CFG-path drop tracking, closure-capture UAF, for_iter_init alias, ~25ns/store perf cliff, W8 RC mismatch). The iter-88 attempt resulted in 33 UAFs and was immediately reverted. The design doc itself says 'must-fix issues found -- resolve BEFORE coding' and 'ship A+B together behind a NEW flag.' This is an irreducibly complex all-or-nothing change that has already failed once. Estimating 4-5 iterations for a change with 7 known blockers that previously produced 33 UAFs on its first attempt is optimistic by at least 2x. More critically, if scope-exit RC destabilizes during Phase 3 work and forces a revert, every test that Phase 3 added must be re-validated under both RC modes -- the blast radius scales with how much Forge code exists.
issues.fix: Separate scope-exit RC into its own dedicated campaign with no Forge interleaving. Do not estimate 4-5 iterations -- estimate 8-12 with explicit go/no-go gates at each adversary finding. The arena path is sufficient for Forge v0.1; scope-exit RC is v0.2.

issues.title: The '~41 strings/request leak' is handwaved as 'tolerable for dev + moderate load' but the mitigation (max_keepalive_reqs) does not exist
issues.detail: The plan repeatedly cites max_keepalive_reqs as the load-bearing leak mitigation. But forge.nova has zero keep-alive support. Every response includes 'Connection: close' (line 47, 154). There is no keep-alive loop, no max_keepalive_reqs cap, no connection reuse. The plan's Phase 1 item #9 says 'Keep-alive loop with max_keepalive_reqs cap (leak mitigation)' -- so the mitigation for the known leak is itself an unbuilt Phase 1 deliverable. Until keep-alive exists, EVERY request opens a new TCP connection, and the ~41 strings/request leak accumulates in the PROCESS, not in a connection scope. Without keep-alive, the arena path frees per-request, so the leak is only on the non-arena path. But the plan's Phase 1 typed core (Request/Response structs) likely cannot use the arena path because struct types need to survive beyond arena_exit for the typed middleware chain. This creates a catch-22: the typed Forge needs the leak mitigation, the leak mitigation needs keep-alive, and keep-alive needs spawn-per-connection (which is also unbuilt).
issues.fix: Acknowledge the dependency chain: spawn-per-connection -> keep-alive -> max_keepalive_reqs -> leak tolerable. All three are Phase 0/1 prerequisites. The arena path may not work for the typed struct model (structs allocated in arena die at arena_exit, but middleware needs to read the Response after the handler returns). Verify arena compatibility with the typed model before committing to it.

issues.title: Performance Stage 2 is REVERTED and the failure mechanism is not understood -- plan treats it as 're-validate' work
issues.detail: Stage 2 (unbox typed struct fields) was attempted, caused nn/stats tests to fail under parallel load but pass in isolation, and was reverted. The plan says 'S2 re-validate' as if it is bounded cleanup. But the failure mode -- load-dependent flake where deterministic codegen produces different runtime behavior under parallel test execution -- is not diagnosed. The PERFORMANCE_SPECIALIZATION.md says 'the load-dependence still needs explaining (rule out a green-runtime/heap-layout interaction).' If the failure is a heap-layout-dependent UB in the float unboxing path, it could be a latent soundness bug in the value model exposed by Stage 2, not a Stage 2 bug per se. The plan puts S2 at ~5 iterations alongside Phase 1; if the root cause is a green-runtime memory ordering issue, it could be weeks of debugging that blocks the Tier-3 gate for everything else.
issues.fix: Do not schedule S2 re-validation during Forge Phase 1. Diagnose the nn/stats parallel flake first as a standalone investigation. If the root cause is heap-layout-dependent UB, it is a soundness bug that must be fixed regardless of S2.

issues.title: Plan claims 'MATCH' or 'WIN' on 8/20 framework dimensions today but actual forge.nova is a 562-line string-surgery MVP
issues.detail: The competitive scorecard claims Forge TODAY wins on: startup time, memory baseline, single binary deploy, handler simplicity, 10k concurrent, crash isolation, GC impact, JSON from domain type. But: (1) 10k concurrent is false -- serve() is synchronous, no spawn. (2) Crash isolation is false in Forge -- recover() middleware is described in FORGE_DESIGN.md but does not exist in forge.nova; the crash_isolation_test is a core NOVA test, not a Forge test. (3) JSON from domain type requires json_of(status, value) with explicit status code, not 'return user' as the plan claims. (4) Handler simplicity: handlers take (method, path, body) as THREE STRING ARGS, not a typed Request -- 'fn(m, p, b)' is NOT 'Flask-simple.' (5) GC impact: only the arena path (serve_n_arena) is proven flat; the non-arena serve path leaks. The honest scorecard is closer to 4/20 today (startup, memory baseline, single binary, compile-time DI), not 8/20.
issues.fix: Rewrite the competitive scorecard with a 'TODAY (proven in forge.nova code)' column vs 'PLAN (designed but unbuilt)' column. Do not claim 'WIN' for capabilities that exist only as core NOVA primitives but are not wired into the Forge serving path.

issues.title: The forge/ migration plan touches ~40 files in one atomic commit and is deferred to 'after Phase 1' -- blast radius on 448-gate
issues.detail: The plan says: 'Create nova-compiler/forge/ with src/forge.nova... Update resolve_module_file search order... Move forge.nova and forge_*_test.nova files... Update all imports in ~40 demo files... Run full 448-test regression -- must pass in the SAME commit.' This is a 40+ file rename commit that changes module resolution. If ANY of the 40 import updates is wrong, or if the module resolution change has an edge case, the regression drops. The plan says 'after Phase 1 (typed core) is complete' -- meaning after adding 17 new deliverables to forge.nova, making it much larger and more import-dependent. The blast radius grows with delay. Also, the module resolution change (adding stdlib/ and nova_packages/ to the search path) is a compiler change requiring Tier-3 reconverge, which the plan does not flag. A 40-file rename + module resolution change + reconverge in one commit is not 'safe' -- it is the highest-risk kind of commit.
issues.fix: Do the forge/ migration BEFORE Phase 1, not after. The current forge.nova is small (562 lines) with few dependents. Every Phase 1 deliverable makes migration harder. Split into two commits: (1) module resolution change + reconverge, (2) file moves + import updates.

issues.title: Phase 3 OpenAPI generation at compile time requires AST/type information the compiler does not expose
issues.detail: Phase 3 item #9 says 'OpenAPI 3.x generation at compile time from route signatures + types.' This requires the compiler to: (a) identify which functions are Forge route handlers, (b) extract their parameter types and return types, (c) generate an OpenAPI JSON schema from struct definitions, (d) embed it in the binary. The NOVA compiler is a self-hosting compiler written in NOVA (~15.5K lines) that emits LLVM IR. It has no plugin system, no macro system, no build-step hook, and no way for user code to introspect the compiler's type environment at compile time. The plan says 'Compile-time route analysis (build-step AST walk)' as the core work, but this requires either: (1) a new compiler pass that understands Forge's routing API (coupling the compiler to a framework), or (2) a build-step tool that parses NOVA source and extracts route/type info (a second parser). Both are significant multi-iteration efforts that the plan estimates as part of an '8-12 iteration' phase containing 19 other deliverables.
issues.fix: Descope compile-time OpenAPI from Phase 3. Runtime OpenAPI generation (like FastAPI) is achievable with the RTTI metadata that already exists. Compile-time generation is a Phase 5+ endgame feature requiring compiler infrastructure that does not exist.

issues.title: Parallelization claim: 'Core A3 (multicore) parallelizes with Forge Phases 1-2' ignores that both touch nova_runtime.c
issues.detail: The plan says multicore scheduler work (A3) is 'a RUNTIME change (zero compiler touch)' that can proceed on a separate track. But Forge Phase 1 also touches the runtime: spawn-per-connection requires changes to the serve path in nova_runtime.c (or at minimum, new runtime builtins like recv_request_timeout). The multicore work changes nova_sched_spawn, the run-queue, carrier threads, and the park/unpark mechanism -- exactly the primitives that spawn-per-connection depends on. If A3 step 1 (global-locked run-queue + 2 carriers) changes the scheduling semantics, it can break Forge's spawn-per-connection serving. Both are Tier-2 gated (runtime-only), and the plan says 'exactly one reconverge in flight' -- but with two teams of changes hitting the same runtime file, merge conflicts and interaction bugs are likely. The 15 pre-catalogued races in A3 specifically include 'parker vs waker overlap' which is exactly the pattern that spawn-per-connection + arena interaction would trigger.
issues.fix: Serialize A3 and Forge Phase 1. Complete spawn-per-connection on the N=1 single-carrier scheduler first (proven stable). Then start A3 multicore wiring. Alternatively, accept that A3 is Phase 7 (throughput benchmarks) and not needed for Forge v0.1.

issues.title: No user/developer testing or feedback loop anywhere in the plan -- 'M5: 10 real applications by external developers' is Phase 7
issues.detail: The plan's first mention of external developers is Phase 7, item #6: '10 real applications by external developers.' By Phase 7, the estimated calendar time is 18-24 months solo. The plan builds an entire framework + ORM + auth + sessions + OpenAPI + TypeScript client generation + LiveView + WASM frontend before ANY external developer touches the code. This is the classic 'build it and they will come' anti-pattern. Every assumption about what developers want (the handler API shape, the forge.get free-function syntax, the 'no template language' decision, the structs-not-ORM data model) is untested with real users. The plan explicitly says 'forge.get(app, ...) is one token more than Flask per route -- this is honest and unavoidable, not a stylistic choice' -- but has zero evidence that developers will accept this tradeoff. The forge/ README, getting-started guide, and installation binary are not mentioned until Phase 4 (scaffolding) or Phase 7 (documentation). A developer who downloads NOVA today gets a Windows exe with no documentation, no error messages pointing to docs, and a 562-line forge.nova that uses string-based handlers.
issues.fix: Add an 'M0.5: External developer smoke test' milestone after Phase 1. Get 3-5 developers to build a TODO API with Forge and collect feedback on: installation, error messages, handler API shape, data access ergonomics, and deployment. Use feedback to validate or revise Phases 2-3 before building them.

issues.title: Postgres promoted to Phase 1.5 but the libpq FFI pattern requires link-time dependency -- violates 'zero-dependency single binary' moat
issues.detail: Phase 1.5 says 'libpq FFI binding (connect/query/exec/prepare/finish)' with '@link("pq") FFI pattern (already proven with SQLite).' But libpq is a shared library that must be installed on the target system. A NOVA binary linked against libpq requires libpq.so/libpq.dll on the deployment target. This directly contradicts Moat 1 ('zero-dependency single static binary, scp myapp server: and run'). SQLite is statically linkable (it is a single C file); Postgres is not (libpq depends on OpenSSL, libcrypto, and system DNS). The plan does not acknowledge this contradiction. The 'one binary, zero deps' promise works for SQLite but breaks the moment you add Postgres.
issues.fix: Either: (1) implement a native Postgres wire protocol in NOVA/C (no libpq dependency, but significant effort -- Postgres wire protocol is complex), or (2) acknowledge that Postgres apps need libpq on the target and update the 'zero-dependency' claim to 'zero-dependency for SQLite apps; libpq required for Postgres.' Option 1 is the only path consistent with the moat claim.

issues.title: The plan's timeline ('6-10 months solo to production-viable') is based on iteration counts that do not match observed velocity
issues.detail: The plan estimates M2 (production-viable) at 16-25 iterations over 12-20 weeks. This implies ~1.2 iterations per week. But the actual git history shows 522 commits in 15 days (June 1-16), which is ~35 commits/day. An 'iteration' in NOVA's history maps to ~3-8 commits (the iter-87 through iter-101 span covers ~14 iterations over ~8 days). This is ~1.75 iterations per day, or ~12/week -- 10x the plan's estimate. However, this velocity was achieved during an intense AI-assisted sprint on core language work. Forge framework work (pure NOVA, Tier-0) has different characteristics: it involves designing APIs, writing docs, testing against real HTTP clients, and iterating on DX -- none of which benefit from the compiler-sprint velocity. The plan's timeline is plausible for compiler work but likely underestimates framework design and testing work by 2-3x.
issues.fix: Separate timeline estimates for compiler work (high velocity, AI-assisted) vs framework design work (lower velocity, requires manual HTTP testing, DX iteration). Phase 1 is mostly framework work and should be estimated at 2-3 weeks, not 4-6 weeks.

issues.title: Backend-only mode (microservices) has no service mesh, no health check, no graceful shutdown until Phase 2-3
issues.detail: The plan says 'backend-only mode reaches production-viable (Phase 3) 2-3 phases before full-stack.' But 'production-viable backend' requires at minimum: health checks (Phase 2 #10), graceful shutdown (Phase 2 #15), security headers (Phase 2 #12), and rate limiting (Phase 2 #13). These are all Phase 2 deliverables. Phase 1 (M1: BACKEND-USABLE) has: routing, typed Request/Response, crash isolation, and static serving. This is 'demo-usable,' not 'production-usable.' A team evaluating Forge at M1 finds: no health checks for k8s, no graceful shutdown (kill -9 drops in-flight requests), no rate limiting (trivial DoS), no security headers (fails any security audit). Calling M1 'BACKEND-USABLE' is misleading -- it is 'BACKEND-DEMOABLE.'
issues.fix: Rename M1 to 'BACKEND-DEMOABLE' and promote health check + graceful shutdown to Phase 1 (they are ~20 lines each in the non-arena serve path). Rate limiting and security headers can stay Phase 2.

issues.title: Phase 6.5 (distributed microservices) depends on remote_spawn which is 'still a stub'
issues.detail: Phase 6.5 ('THE Structural Moat') includes 'Location-transparent channels (call process on any node, compiler routes)' and 'Service discovery (process registry + health check).' The plan's own memory says 'remote_spawn still a stub' (MEMORY.md distributed channels entry). Location-transparent channels require remote_spawn to place processes on remote nodes. The plan lists this as the phase that 'structurally beats Spring Cloud' but it depends on core distributed primitives that are stubs. The distance between 'TCP + length-prefixed JSON point-to-point' (what exists) and 'location-transparent channels with automatic tracing' (what Phase 6.5 needs) is enormous -- it includes: serialization format negotiation, failure detection, reconnection, load balancing, and name resolution. Each of these is a multi-iteration effort.
issues.fix: Phase 6.5 is not 5-6 items in one phase. It is 3-4 phases of distributed systems work. Rename it to 'Phase 6.5-8' and acknowledge the remote_spawn stub. Do not claim 'structurally beats Spring Cloud' until remote_spawn + service discovery are proven.

issues.title: The plan's innovation claims include 'Channel-Graph Distributed Tracing (world-first)' but no tracing infrastructure exists
issues.detail: Innovation 4 says 'distributed traces are automatic... the process/channel topology IS the trace.' This is architecturally plausible but zero tracing code exists. There is no trace-id propagation, no span emission, no trace collection, no trace visualization. The 'world-first' claim is made for a feature that is pure design. The plan does not specify WHERE traces are collected (in-memory? exported to file? OpenTelemetry-compatible?), HOW channel sends propagate trace context (every send copies a trace-id? that is overhead), or WHAT happens when a channel crosses machine boundaries (the remote_* path serializes as JSON -- no trace metadata is included). Calling this a 'shipped innovation' in the same section as actually-shipped innovations (RTTI, arena, RC) conflates aspiration with reality.
issues.fix: Move Innovation 4 to a 'PLANNED' section, separate from 'SHIPPED' innovations. Do not use 'world-first' for unbuilt features.

verdict: This plan is a detailed, grounded document that correctly identifies NOVA's structural moats and sequences the work logically. It is better than 90% of language project plans because it acknowledges real gaps (the leak, the return-site hook, the RTTI boundary). But it has a FATAL flaw that would stall the loop: spawn-per-connection does not exist in forge.nova, yet the plan treats it as a Tier-0 'pure NOVA' change inside Phase 1. It is actually a structural rearchitecture of the serve+arena interaction that touches the most dangerous part of the system (green scheduler + arena memory + concurrent tasks). If this stalls, everything from Phase 1 onward is blocked. The plan also systematically overstates what is 'PROVEN' vs 'DESIGNED' -- the competitive scorecard claims 8/20 wins today but only 4 are real in forge.nova code. The scope-exit RC estimate (4-5 iterations for a change with 7 unresolved adversary findings that previously produced 33 UAFs) is dangerously optimistic. The biggest risk to the unstoppable loop is not any single technical problem -- it is the plan's habit of promoting designs to claims, which leads to building on assumptions that turn out to be false (exactly what happened with iter-88's scope-exit RC and Stage 2's parallel flake). The loop stays fast ONLY if the plan stops saying 'PROVEN' for things that are 'DESIGNED' and treats spawn-per-connection + arena interaction as the Phase 0 blocker it actually is.
